name: Healthcare IT Risk
description: Healthcare IT risk controls built on the HIPAA Security, Privacy and Breach Notification Rules, extended to clinical systems, medical devices, business associates and clinical downtime. Suited to providers, payers and health tech business associates.
references: HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), HITECH, HHS 405(d) HICP, 21st Century Cures Act (45 CFR Part 171), FDA FD&C Act 524B, HITRUST CSF

categories.name: HIPAA Governance & Risk Analysis
categories.objective: The Security Rule's administrative safeguards are in place and driven by an accurate, current risk analysis.

items.control: An enterprise-wide security risk analysis covers every system that creates, receives, maintains or transmits ePHI, and is updated annually and on significant change.
items.risk: Unassessed ePHI systems leave risks unmanaged. Missing or incomplete risk analyses are the most frequently cited finding in OCR enforcement.
items.test: Compare systems in the risk analysis to the ePHI system inventory, and confirm the analysis covers threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact and is dated within 12 months.
evidence: Security risk analysis report with ePHI system inventory
Change-triggered update records (e.g. new EHR module, acquisition)

items.control: A risk management plan reduces identified risks to a reasonable and appropriate level, with owners, dates and progress tracking.
items.risk: Risks are identified but never remediated.
items.test: For High risks in the analysis, confirm a plan entry with owner and target date, and evidence of progress each quarter.

items.control: A Security Official and a Privacy Official are formally designated, with documented responsibilities.
items.risk: No one is accountable for HIPAA compliance.
items.test: Inspect designation letters and job descriptions, and confirm the designees are current employees.

items.control: HIPAA policies and procedures are documented, reviewed periodically, available to the workforce and retained for six years.
items.risk: The organisation cannot demonstrate compliance to OCR.
items.test: Inspect the policy library for review dates and the retention of superseded versions for six years.

items.control: A sanction policy is applied consistently to workforce members who violate security or privacy policies, and sanctions are documented.
items.risk: Violations recur because there are no consequences.
items.test: For confirmed privacy violations in the period, trace each to a documented sanction consistent with the policy.

items.control: The workforce, including physicians, students and volunteers, completes HIPAA security and privacy training at onboarding and annually.
items.risk: Staff mishandle PHI or fall for phishing.
items.test: Compare LMS completion records to the HR and medical staff roster, and confirm new hires completed training before EHR access.
evidence: LMS completion report compared to workforce roster
Training content covering phishing, minimum necessary and incident reporting
Comparison of training date to EHR access date for new hires

items.control: Technical and non-technical evaluations of HIPAA safeguards are performed periodically and after significant operational change.
items.risk: Safeguards drift out of compliance unnoticed.
items.test: Inspect the latest evaluation report and confirm findings were tracked to closure.
evidence: HIPAA evaluation or gap assessment report

categories.name: Access Control
categories.objective: Access to ePHI is unique, role-based, strongly authenticated, promptly removed and physically protected.

items.control: Every EHR and ePHI system user has a unique user ID, and there are no shared clinical logins.
items.risk: Access to patient records cannot be attributed to an individual.
items.test: Inspect EHR and ePHI application user lists for generic or shared accounts, and review exceptions.
evidence: EHR user listing (e.g. Epic, Oracle Health)

items.control: EHR access is role-based in line with the minimum necessary standard, and role assignments are reviewed at least annually.
items.risk: Staff can view far more patient information than their job requires.
items.test: Inspect the EHR role-to-job matrix and, for a sample of users, confirm the assigned template matches the job code.
evidence: EHR security template to job code matrix
Annual role review sign-off by department

items.control: Emergency (break-the-glass) access requires a recorded reason, and every use is reviewed by Privacy within a set timeframe.
items.risk: Emergency access is used to snoop on records.
items.test: Inspect the break-the-glass report for the period and confirm each event was reviewed and inappropriate use investigated.

items.control: MFA is required for remote access to ePHI, EHR administration, email and electronic prescribing of controlled substances (EPCS).
items.risk: Stolen credentials give remote access to patient data, or allow fraudulent controlled-substance prescriptions.
items.test: Inspect remote access and IdP MFA policies and EPCS two-factor configuration, and compare enrollment to in-scope users.
evidence: Remote access and IdP MFA policy

items.control: Shared clinical workstations lock or log off automatically after inactivity, with fast user switching (e.g. badge tap) for clinicians.
items.risk: Unattended sessions expose patient records to passers-by.
items.test: Inspect timeout settings for clinical workstation policies and observe a sample of workstations in clinical areas.
evidence: Group policy or MDM session timeout settings
Single sign-on and badge-tap configuration (e.g. Imprivata)

items.control: Access is removed promptly on termination, including for affiliated physicians, residents, students and agency staff.
items.risk: Former workforce or affiliates keep access to patient records.
items.test: For 25 terminations across employees and affiliates, compare termination date to EHR and directory disable dates.
evidence: HR and medical staff termination reports

items.control: Physical access to data centres, network closets and records rooms is badge-controlled and reviewed, and workstations are positioned away from public view.
items.risk: Unauthorised people physically access ePHI systems or records.
items.test: Inspect badge access lists for restricted areas and the quarterly review, and walk through sampled clinical areas.
evidence: Badge access list for restricted areas

categories.name: Monitoring & Logging
categories.objective: Access to ePHI and security events are logged, reviewed and acted on.

items.control: Audit logging is enabled in the EHR and ePHI systems for record access, view, modify, print and export, and logs are retained six years.
items.risk: Inappropriate access cannot be detected or investigated.
items.test: Inspect audit configuration for sampled ePHI systems, retrieve an access log for a test patient, and confirm retention.
evidence: Access log for a test patient

items.control: Privacy monitoring reviews EHR access for snooping (employee, VIP, family member and same-surname records), and alerts are investigated.
items.risk: Employees view records of celebrities, colleagues or relatives without a work reason.
items.test: Inspect privacy monitoring rules and, for sampled alerts, confirm investigation, outcome and sanction where appropriate.
evidence: Privacy monitoring rule set (e.g. Protenus, Imprivata FairWarning, Epic access audit)

items.control: Failed login attempts and anomalous access (impossible travel, off-hours bulk access) raise alerts that are investigated.
items.risk: Credential attacks and compromised accounts go unnoticed.
items.test: Inspect alert rules for failed logins and anomalous access, and trace sampled alerts to investigation records.

items.control: EDR and 24x7 security monitoring cover clinical and business endpoints and servers.
items.risk: Ransomware spreads through clinical systems before anyone responds.
items.test: Compare EDR coverage to the asset inventory (excluding validated medical devices), and inspect the SOC or MDR SLA report.
evidence: Exceptions for devices that cannot run agents

categories.name: Data Protection & Integrity
categories.objective: ePHI is encrypted, transmitted securely, kept accurate and matched to the right patient.

items.control: ePHI is encrypted in transit using TLS, secure messaging or Direct for all external and wireless transmission.
items.risk: PHI is intercepted in transit.
items.test: Run a TLS scan of external endpoints and inspect interface engine and SFTP configuration for encryption.

items.control: ePHI is encrypted at rest on laptops, mobile devices, removable media and databases to meet the HHS breach safe harbor guidance.
items.risk: A lost or stolen device becomes a reportable breach.
items.test: Inspect the encryption compliance report for laptops and mobile devices and encryption settings for ePHI databases.
evidence: Mobile device encryption enforcement in MDM

items.control: Device and media movements are logged, and media are sanitised before reuse or disposal.
items.risk: PHI is left on disposed copiers, drives or devices.
items.test: Trace a sample of disposed devices (including copiers and imaging equipment) to sanitisation certificates.
evidence: Copier and imaging device hard drive procedure

items.control: Clinicians use an approved secure messaging app for PHI, and PHI over consumer SMS or personal email is prohibited and monitored.
items.risk: PHI is sent through insecure consumer channels.
items.test: Inspect the communications policy, secure messaging adoption report and DLP alerts for PHI sent to personal email.
evidence: Secure messaging adoption report (e.g. TigerConnect, Epic Secure Chat)
DLP alerts for PHI to personal email

items.control: Integrity controls prevent improper alteration of ePHI: chart amendments are tracked, and HL7 and FHIR interface messages are validated with error queues worked daily.
items.risk: Clinical data is altered or lost in transit, affecting patient care.
items.test: Inspect the amendment audit trail for a sample of records, and interface error queue reports for a sample of days.
evidence: Interface engine error queue reports (e.g. Rhapsody, Cloverleaf, Mirth)

items.control: Patient identity matching is controlled through the EMPI, and duplicate and overlaid medical record numbers are monitored and resolved.
items.risk: Records are merged into the wrong patient, causing clinical and privacy harm.
items.test: Inspect the duplicate rate trend and, for sampled merges, confirm review and correct resolution.

categories.name: Change Management & Clinical Systems
categories.objective: Changes to the EHR, interfaces, clinical content and decision support are tested, clinically validated and approved.

items.control: EHR changes and upgrades go through change management with testing, clinical validation and planned downtime communication.
items.risk: Untested EHR changes disrupt care or introduce patient safety errors.
items.test: For sampled EHR changes, confirm testing evidence, clinical sign-off and approval before migration to production.
evidence: Change tickets with test scripts and results

items.control: Interface changes (new feeds, mapping changes) are tested end to end with message validation before go-live.
items.risk: Interface changes drop or misroute clinical results.
items.test: For sampled interface changes, inspect end-to-end test results and sign-off by the receiving department.

items.control: Changes to clinical content (order sets, alerts, documentation templates) are approved by a clinical governance committee.
items.risk: Unvetted clinical content leads to inappropriate orders or alert fatigue.
items.test: For sampled clinical content changes, confirm committee approval before build.

items.control: Clinical decision support and AI tools are validated for safety, accuracy and bias on local data before go-live, and monitored afterwards.
items.risk: Decision support or AI tools give unsafe or biased recommendations.
items.test: For CDS or AI tools deployed in the period, inspect local validation results, bias assessment and governance approval.
evidence: Clinical governance approval and monitoring plan
items.other: ONC HTI-1 decision support interventions; FDA CDS guidance

categories.name: Medical Device Security
categories.objective: Connected medical devices are inventoried, segmented, vetted before purchase and patched with the manufacturer.

items.control: Network-connected medical devices are inventoried with OS, software bill of materials (SBOM), ePHI storage, location and owner.
items.risk: Vulnerable devices are unknown and unprotected.
items.test: Compare passive discovery output to the clinical engineering inventory and investigate unmatched devices.
evidence: Medical device inventory (e.g. Claroty, Armis, Ordr discovery)
Reconciliation to the clinical engineering CMMS

items.control: Medical devices are on segmented networks, and legacy devices that cannot be patched have documented compensating controls.
items.risk: A compromised device is used to reach the wider network, or the network is used to attack devices.
items.test: Inspect segmentation rules for device VLANs and risk acceptances for legacy devices.

items.control: Devices and clinical applications receive a cybersecurity review before purchase, covering MDS2, SBOM and patch support commitments.
items.risk: Insecure or unsupportable devices are purchased.
items.test: For devices purchased in the period, confirm a completed MDS2 and security review before the purchase order date.

items.control: Manufacturer-validated patches are applied, and FDA and CISA medical device advisories are tracked against the inventory.
items.risk: Known device vulnerabilities stay unpatched.
items.test: For recent advisories, confirm exposure was checked against the inventory and remediation tracked.

categories.name: Third-Party Risk & Business Associates
categories.objective: PHI shared with vendors is covered by BAAs, appropriate due diligence and controlled access.

items.control: All business associates and vendors that create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI are inventoried.
items.risk: PHI is shared with vendors no one is overseeing.
items.test: Compare the BA inventory to accounts payable vendors and IT integrations to find missing business associates.
evidence: Reconciliation to accounts payable and interface lists

items.control: A BAA containing the required provisions is executed before any PHI is disclosed.
items.risk: PHI is disclosed without a BAA. This is a common OCR finding.
items.test: For BAs onboarded in the period, confirm the BAA signature date precedes the first PHI exchange.
evidence: First data exchange date per BA

items.control: Business associates are security-reviewed in proportion to risk (questionnaire, HITRUST or SOC 2 report).
items.risk: A BA with weak security causes a breach of the organisation's PHI.
items.test: For sampled high-risk BAs, inspect the latest assessment or certification review.
evidence: HITRUST or SOC 2 report review memos

items.control: Business associates are contractually required to flow BAA obligations down to their subcontractors.
items.risk: PHI reaches downstream subcontractors without protections.
items.test: Inspect sampled BAAs for subcontractor flow-down clauses.

items.control: Vendor remote access to clinical systems is MFA-protected, time-bound, approved per session and recorded.
items.risk: Vendor access is used as an entry point for ransomware.
items.test: Inspect vendor access platform settings and sampled sessions for approval, MFA and recording.
evidence: Vendor account list with expiry dates

items.control: When a BA relationship ends, PHI is returned or destroyed with certification, and access is revoked.
items.risk: Former vendors retain PHI and access.
items.test: For BAs terminated in the period, inspect the return or destruction certificate and access removal.

categories.name: Contingency Planning & Clinical Downtime
categories.objective: Patient care continues safely, and ePHI can be recovered, during outages and cyberattacks.

items.control: ePHI backups produce retrievable exact copies, including an immutable copy isolated from the production domain.
items.risk: Ransomware destroys ePHI with no clean copy to restore.
items.test: Inspect backup job success for ePHI systems and immutability configuration.
evidence: Backup job reports for ePHI systems
Backup scope compared to the ePHI inventory

items.control: A disaster recovery plan for the EHR and critical clinical systems defines RTO and RPO, and is tested at least annually.
items.risk: The EHR cannot be restored within clinically safe timeframes.
items.test: Inspect the DR plan and latest test report and compare achieved RTO and RPO to targets.
evidence: RTO and RPO achieved vs target

items.control: Emergency-mode and clinical downtime procedures exist for each department, including paper forms and read-only business continuity access (BCA) workstations that are checked regularly.
items.risk: Care is unsafe during EHR outages because staff cannot access records or orders.
items.test: Inspect departmental downtime procedures and monthly BCA workstation check logs.

items.control: Contingency plans are tested through downtime drills and DR exercises, and revised based on results.
items.risk: Plans fail in a real event because they were never practised.
items.test: Inspect drill reports and confirm resulting plan changes were made.

items.control: An applications and data criticality analysis ranks systems for recovery priority and is approved by clinical leadership.
items.risk: Recovery effort goes to the wrong systems first.
items.test: Inspect the criticality analysis and confirm clinical leadership approval and alignment with DR sequencing.

items.control: A ransomware playbook covers ambulance diversion decisions, patient safety, isolation steps and notification to HHS, the FBI and the state.
items.risk: A ransomware response puts patients at risk and misses obligations.
items.test: Inspect the playbook and the latest tabletop exercise including clinical leadership.
evidence: Tabletop exercise report with clinical participation

categories.name: Privacy & Breach Notification
categories.objective: Uses and disclosures of PHI are lawful, breaches are assessed and notified on time, and patient rights are honoured.

items.control: Every impermissible use or disclosure gets a documented four-factor breach risk assessment.
items.risk: Reportable breaches are missed, or non-reportable decisions cannot be defended.
items.test: For sampled privacy incidents, confirm a completed four-factor assessment and documented conclusion.

items.control: Breaches are notified to individuals within 60 days of discovery, to HHS and the media as required, and breaches affecting fewer than 500 people are logged for annual HHS reporting.
items.risk: Late or missed notifications lead to OCR penalties.
items.test: For breaches in the period, compare the discovery date to the notification dates, and confirm HHS portal submissions.
evidence: Annual log of breaches affecting fewer than 500 people

items.control: The minimum necessary standard is applied to routine disclosures and requests through documented protocols.
items.risk: More PHI is disclosed than needed.
items.test: Inspect minimum necessary protocols and, for sampled routine disclosures, confirm only the necessary data was released.

items.control: Patient access requests are fulfilled within 30 days, and electronic health information is shared without information blocking.
items.risk: OCR right-of-access enforcement, or information blocking penalties.
items.test: Inspect the access request log for turnaround times and confirm denials or delays used a documented exception.
evidence: Access request log with turnaround times
Patient portal and API availability records

items.control: Data used for analytics and research is de-identified by Safe Harbor or Expert Determination, or covered by authorisation or IRB waiver.
items.risk: Identifiable PHI is used for secondary purposes without permission.
items.test: For sampled research or analytics datasets, confirm the de-identification method or authorisation basis.
evidence: Expert determination report or Safe Harbor checklist

items.control: The Notice of Privacy Practices is current, an accounting of disclosures is available, and privacy complaints are logged and resolved.
items.risk: Patients' privacy rights are not honoured.
items.test: Inspect the NPP for currency and posting, test an accounting-of-disclosures request, and inspect the complaint log.
